name: Regular Expressions
author: Recurse
subject: tools
description: Read and write regex: classes, quantifiers, anchors, groups, backreferences, lookarounds, and regex in Python and JS.

lesson.intro: Regular expressions are a compact language for describing patterns in text: find every order number in a log, check that a ZIP code has the right shape, or turn dates from one format into another. The same syntax works in Python, JavaScript, grep, editors and databases. This lesson builds patterns from the ground up, shows how the matching engine thinks, and ends with when to put regex down and reach for a parser.
objectives: Read and write patterns using literals, escapes, character classes and quantifiers
Predict greedy and lazy matches, and anchor patterns correctly for validation
Capture, reuse and reformat text with groups, alternation, backreferences and lookarounds
Use regex in Python and JavaScript with the right functions and flags
Recognize when a parser or a string method is the better tool

sections.title: Literals and metacharacters
sections.body:
You have a 50,000-line log and need every line with an order number like `ORD-48213`. Searching for the text `ORD-` finds them, but also `ORD-TEST` and a stray `ORD-` at the end of a line. A **regular expression** (regex) is a small language for describing text precisely: `ORD-\d{5}` means "ORD-, then exactly five digits". Regex is built into Python, JavaScript, grep, every serious editor and most databases, so the skill pays off everywhere.

Most characters in a pattern are **literals** that match themselves. The pattern `cat` matches the characters c, a, t in that order, and by default a match can sit **anywhere** in the text, so `cat` also matches inside `concatenate`. The engine scans left to right and reports the first (leftmost) match it finds.

A handful of **metacharacters** have special meanings instead; the table below lists them. The most common is the dot: `.` matches any single character except a newline. So `a.c` matches `abc`, `a-c` and `a c`, but not `ac`, because the dot needs exactly one character to consume.

To match a metacharacter literally, **escape** it with a backslash: `\.` is a real dot, `\$` a dollar sign, `\(` an opening parenthesis and `\\` a backslash. Forgetting to escape is the most common regex bug, and a sneaky one, because the pattern still matches the example you tested: `3.14` happily matches `3.14`, but it also matches `3x14` and `3914`.

When you read someone else's regex, go one piece at a time, left to right, saying out loud what each piece matches. That habit alone catches most mistakes.
sections.code:
Metacharacter   Meaning
.               any one character except a newline
\               escape the next character (or start \d, \w, \b ...)
[ ]             a character class: one character from a set
* + ? { }       quantifiers: how many times the item before repeats
^ $             anchors: start and end of the string
( ) |           groups and alternation

Pattern   Matches            Does not match
a.c       abc, a-c, a c      ac, abbc
3\.14     3.14               3x14, 3914
\$\d      $5, cost $9        5, $x
sections.pitfall: Leaving a dot unescaped in file extensions or IP addresses. The pattern .csv also matches xcsv; write \.csv.

check.question: Which text does the pattern `1+1=2` match?
check.explanation: The + is a quantifier, not a plus sign: 1+ means one or more 1s, followed by the literal text 1=2. So it matches 11=2 (and 111=2) but not the arithmetic 1+1=2. To match a plus sign, escape it: 1\+1=2.

sections.title: Character classes
sections.body:
Product codes start with a letter, phone numbers contain digits, and usernames allow letters, digits and underscores. A **character class** describes a set of allowed characters and matches exactly **one** character from that set.

- `[aeiou]` matches one lowercase vowel.
- `[a-z]` is a range: one lowercase letter. Ranges combine: `[a-zA-Z0-9]` is one letter or digit, and `[0-9a-fA-F]` one hex digit.
- `[^0-9]`, with a caret right after the opening bracket, is **negated**: one character that is *not* a digit.
- Inside brackets most metacharacters are plain characters: `[.]` is a real dot and `[$]` a dollar sign. A hyphen is literal at the start or end (`[-+]`). The ones that still need care are `]`, `\`, a `^` at the start and a `-` in the middle.

Common classes have shorthand forms:

- `\d`: a digit, like `[0-9]`. (In Python 3 it also matches digits from other scripts in Unicode text.)
- `\w`: a word character: a letter, a digit or an underscore.
- `\s`: whitespace: a space, tab or newline.
- `\D`, `\W` and `\S`: the opposites, one character that is not in the lowercase set.

A class is always one character wide. `[0-9]` matches the `4` in `42`, not `42`; to match more you need a quantifier, the topic of the next section.

Prefer a class that says exactly what you mean over the dot. `\d\d:\d\d` matches times like `09:30`, while `..:..` would also accept `ab:cd`.
sections.code:
Text: "Room 4B, floor 2"

Pattern       Matches one...                First match
[0-9]         digit                         4
[A-Z]         uppercase letter              R
[^a-zA-Z ]    character that is not a       4
              letter or a space
\d            digit                         4
\w            letter, digit or _            R
\s            whitespace character          the space after Room
sections.pitfall: Writing [0-F] for hex digits. A range follows character codes, so it includes punctuation such as : ; < = > ? @ and misses lowercase letters. Spell it out: [0-9a-fA-F].

check.question: How many characters does `[A-Za-z0-9_]` match at a time?
choices: Up to four, one from each part
As many as possible in a row
check.explanation: However many ranges you list, a class matches a single character from the combined set. Add a quantifier such as + to match a run of them.

sections.title: Quantifiers: greedy and lazy
sections.body: A ZIP code is five digits, a phone extension one to four digits, a middle name optional. **Quantifiers** say how many times the item just before them may repeat: - `*`: zero or more. `ab*c` matches `ac`, `abc` and `abbbc`. - `+`: one or more. `\d+` matches `7` or `2026`. - `?`: zero or one, in other words optional. `colou?r` matches `color` and `colour`. - `{3}`: exactly three. `{2,4}`: two to four. `{2,}`: two or more. A quantifier applies only to the single item before it: `ab+` means a, then one or more b's. To repeat several characters, group them first: `(ab)+` matches `ababab`. Quantifiers are **greedy** by default. They take as much text as they can, then give characters back one at a time (**backtracking**) only if the rest of the pattern fails. That surprises people with patterns like `<.+>` on the text `bold`: the `.+` runs to the end, then backs up just far enough to find a `>`, which is the *last* one, so the match is all of `bold`, not just ``. There are two fixes: - Make the quantifier **lazy** by adding `?`: `*?`, `+?`, `{2,5}?`. A lazy quantifier takes as little as possible and grows only when it must, so `<.+?>` matches ``. - Even better, use a **negated class** that cannot run past the delimiter: `<[^>]+>` means "one or more characters that are not >". It states the intent clearly and is usually faster, because it never needs to backtrack. Greediness never changes *where* a match starts, only where it ends. The engine still reports the leftmost match; greedy or lazy only decides how long it is.
sections.code: Text: bold <.+> greedy bold runs to the end, backs up to the last > <.+?> lazy stops at the first > <[^>]+> class cannot cross a > Text: 1234567 \d{3,5} greedy 12345 as many as allowed \d{3,5}? lazy 123 as few as allowed
sections.pitfall: Using .* between two delimiters in text that contains several of them. It swallows everything up to the last delimiter; use a negated class such as [^"]* instead.

check.question: What does `a{2,}` require?
choices: Two or more a characters in a row
Exactly two a characters in a row
At most two a characters in a row
Two a characters anywhere in the text
check.explanation: {2,} with no upper bound means "at least two", and like every quantifier it repeats the item directly before it, so the a's must be consecutive.

sections.title: Anchors and word boundaries
sections.body:
A form asks for a 4-digit PIN. Your check uses `\d{4}`, and it happily accepts `12345` and `PIN1234`, because it finds four digits *somewhere* in each. Searching and validating are different jobs, and **anchors** are the difference.

Anchors match a **position**, not a character, so they consume no text:

- `^` matches at the start of the string.
- `$` matches at the end of the string.
- `\b` matches at a **word boundary**: a spot between a word character (`\w`) and a non-word character, or between a word character and the start or end of the string. `\B` matches everywhere else.

So `^\d{4}$` means "start, four digits, end": the whole string must be exactly four digits. Whenever you **validate** input (a ZIP code, a hex color, a username), anchor both ends. When you **search** inside text, leave the anchors off or use `\b`.

Word boundaries find whole words: `\bcat\b` matches `cat` in `the cat sat` and `cat!`, but not in `concatenate` or `cats`. Remember that `\b` only knows about `\w` characters, so in `e-mail` there are boundaries on both sides of the hyphen.

Two details trip people up. Inside brackets, a leading `^` means something completely different: it negates the class. And by default `^` and `$` refer to the whole string; with the **multiline** flag (`m`) they also match at the start and end of every line, which is what you want when scanning a block of text line by line.
sections.code:
Pattern     "1234"   "12345"   "PIN1234"   "12 34"
\d{4}       match    match     match       no
^\d{4}$     match    no        no          no

Pattern     "cat"    "the cat sat"   "concatenate"   "cats"
cat         match    match           match           match
\bcat\b     match    match           no              no
sections.pitfall: Validating with an unanchored pattern. Without ^ and $, the check passes as long as a valid-looking piece appears anywhere in the input.

activity.title: Classes, quantifiers and anchors
activity.prompt: Solve each puzzle using only what you have learned so far: classes, quantifiers and anchors. Read the do-not-match list carefully; each entry is there to catch a pattern that is too loose, usually a missing anchor or an unescaped character.

puzzles.prompt: Match times like 9:05 or 23:59: one or two digits, a colon, exactly two digits, and nothing else.
puzzles.hint: \d{1,2} allows one or two digits. Anchor both ends so 123:45 cannot sneak through.

puzzles.prompt: Match lines that are comments: optional spaces, then #.
puzzles.hint: Anchor to the start with ^, allow \s* for the indentation, then a literal #.

puzzles.prompt: Match product codes: two uppercase letters, a dash, then 3 to 5 digits, nothing more.
puzzles.hint: [A-Z]{2} for the letters, a literal dash, \d{3,5} for the digits, and ^ and $ around it all.

puzzles.prompt: Match strings that contain no digits at all.
puzzles.hint: \D is any non-digit. Repeat it and anchor both ends, so every character must be a non-digit.

check.question: Where does `\b` match in the text `hi there`?
choices: At the space, and nowhere else
Only at the very start and end
Before and after each word: four spots
check.explanation: A boundary sits wherever a word character meets a non-word character or an end of the string: before h, after i, before t and after the final e. The space itself is not a boundary; the positions on either side of it are.

sections.title: Groups, alternation and backreferences
sections.body:
You need the year, month and day out of `2026-10-15`, or you want to turn `YYYY-MM-DD` dates into `DD/MM/YYYY`. Parentheses do both: they group parts of a pattern and remember what each part matched.

**Capturing groups** `( )` save the text they match, numbered from 1 in the order of their opening parentheses. In `(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})`, group 1 is the year, group 2 the month and group 3 the day. You can read them in code, or insert them in a replacement string: `$1` in JavaScript, `\1` or `\g<1>` in Python.

**Named groups** make long patterns readable. JavaScript writes them `(?<year>\d{4})` and reads them as `match.groups.year`. Python writes them `(?P<year>\d{4})` and reads `match["year"]` or `match.group("year")`.

**Non-capturing groups** `(?:...)` group without saving, for when you only need the grouping, as in `(?:ab)+`. They keep the numbers of the groups you care about simple.

**Alternation** `|` means "or": `cat|dog` matches either word. It has the **lowest precedence** of anything in a regex, so `^cat|dog$` means "`^cat` or `dog$`", not "exactly cat or dog". Wrap the alternatives in a group to limit them: `^(cat|dog)$`, or `\.(png|jpg|gif)$` for image file names.

A **backreference** `\1` inside the pattern means "the exact text group 1 matched, again". `\b(\w+) \1\b` finds doubled words like `the the`, and `(['"]).*?\1` matches a quoted string that closes with the same kind of quote it opened with. Note the difference: `\1` inside a pattern matches repeated text, while `$1` (JavaScript) or `\1` (Python) in a *replacement* inserts the captured text.
sections.pitfall: Forgetting that | splits the whole pattern. ^cat|dog$ accepts catapult and hotdog; group the alternatives as ^(cat|dog)$.

check.question: In the pattern `((a)(b))c`, which group captures `b`?
check.explanation: Groups are numbered by their opening parentheses from left to right: group 1 is the outer (ab), group 2 is (a) and group 3 is (b). Group 0 is the whole match, abc.

sections.title: Lookahead and lookbehind
sections.body:
A password rule says: at least 8 characters, with at least one digit somewhere. "8 or more characters" is easy (`.{8,}`) and so is "contains a digit" (`\d`), but a plain pattern that checks both at once, with the digit allowed anywhere, gets messy fast. **Lookarounds** solve exactly this kind of problem.

A **lookahead** checks what comes next without consuming it. Like an anchor it is **zero-width**: it tests a condition at the current position, and matching continues from that same spot.

- `(?=...)` is a positive lookahead: what follows must match.
- `(?!...)` is a negative lookahead: what follows must *not* match.

So `^(?=.*\d).{8,}$` reads: at the start, peek ahead for a digit anywhere; if there is one, match 8 or more characters to the end. Stack lookaheads to add rules: `^(?=.*\d)(?=.*[A-Z]).{8,}$` also demands an uppercase letter. Each lookahead runs from the same starting position, independently of the others.

Negative lookahead excludes things. `^(?!test)\w+$` matches words that do not start with `test`. `\d+(?!%)` looks for numbers that are not percentages, but careful: in `50%` it still matches `5`, because that 5 is followed by 0, not %. Writing `\d+(?![\d%])` closes the gap.

Lookahead also extracts a value by what follows it: `\d+(?=EUR)` in `price: 100USD 200EUR` matches `200`, and `EUR` is not part of the match.

**Lookbehind** checks what comes before: `(?<=\$)\d+` matches the digits after a dollar sign without the sign, and `(?<!-)\b\d+` skips negative numbers. JavaScript and Python both support it, though Python requires a lookbehind to have a fixed width.

Use lookarounds sparingly. A rule written as three short checks in code is often easier to read and maintain than one clever pattern.
sections.code:
Pattern               Text                    Result
\d+(?=EUR)            price: 100USD 200EUR    200
(?<=\$)\d+            total $45               45
^(?=.*\d).{8,}$       secret12                match
^(?=.*\d).{8,}$       longpassword            no match: no digit
^(?!test)\w+$         testing                 no match
^(?!test)\w+$         contest                 match
sections.pitfall: Expecting a lookahead to become part of the match. It only checks: \d+(?=EUR) returns 200, not 200EUR. Put text outside the lookahead if you want it included.

activity.title: Groups and lookarounds
activity.prompt: These puzzles need groups, alternation, a backreference and lookaheads. For the password, write the length rule first, then add (?=...) for the digit and watch the failing cases turn green.

puzzles.prompt: Match text where the same word appears twice in a row, like "the the".
puzzles.hint: Capture a word with (\w+), then \1 means "that same text again". Add \b at both ends so "then the" does not count.

puzzles.prompt: Match US ZIP codes: 5 digits, optionally followed by a dash and 4 more digits.
puzzles.hint: Group the optional part and put ? after the group: (-\d{4})?. Anchor both ends.

puzzles.prompt: Match file names ending in .png, .jpg or .gif.
puzzles.hint: Escape the dot, put the alternatives in a group, and anchor the end: \.(png|jpg|gif)$

puzzles.prompt: Match passwords of at least 8 characters that contain at least one digit.
puzzles.hint: Write the length rule first: ^.{8,}$. Then add a lookahead right after ^ that peeks for a digit: (?=.*\d).

puzzles.prompt: Match strings that start with Java, unless it is JavaScript.
puzzles.hint: After ^Java, a negative lookahead (?!Script) rejects the match when Script comes next.

check.question: What does `^(?=.*[A-Z]).{6,}$` require?
choices: At least 6 characters, with an uppercase letter somewhere
At least 6 characters, starting with an uppercase letter
Exactly 6 characters, all of them uppercase letters
An uppercase letter followed by at least 6 more characters
check.explanation: The lookahead peeks from the start for any uppercase letter (.* lets it be anywhere) without consuming anything. Then .{6,}$ matches the whole string, which must be at least 6 characters long.

sections.title: Flags, and regex in Python and JavaScript
sections.body:
The pattern ideas are the same everywhere, but each language wraps them differently, and **flags** change how a pattern behaves:

- `i`: ignore case, so `/error/i` matches `ERROR` and `Error`.
- `g` (JavaScript): global, find every match instead of stopping at the first.
- `m`: multiline, so `^` and `$` also match at the start and end of each line.
- `s`: dotall, so `.` matches newlines too.

**JavaScript** writes patterns as literals between slashes, flags after: `/\d+/g`. The main methods:

- `re.test(str)` returns true or false.
- `str.match(re)` returns the first match and its groups (or `null`); with `g` it returns an array of every matched string.
- `str.matchAll(re)` (requires `g`) yields every match with its groups.
- `str.replace(re, replacement)` replaces the first match, or all of them with `g`.

One trap: a regex with the `g` flag remembers where it stopped in its `lastIndex` property, so calling `test` repeatedly on the same string can return `true` and then `false`. Do not reuse a global regex for repeated `test` calls.

**Python** uses the `re` module. Always write patterns as **raw strings**, `r"\d+"`, so Python does not process the backslashes before the regex engine sees them. Flags are arguments such as `re.IGNORECASE` and `re.MULTILINE`. The functions:

- `re.search(p, s)`: the first match anywhere, or `None`.
- `re.match(p, s)`: a match only at the **start** of the string. `re.fullmatch(p, s)`: the whole string must match, ideal for validation.
- `re.findall(p, s)`: a list of all matches, or of the group's text when the pattern has one group.
- `re.sub(p, repl, s)`: replace every match; `\1` or `\g<1>` in `repl` inserts a group.
- `re.compile(p)`: a reusable pattern object for a pattern you use many times.

A match object gives `.group()` for the whole match, `.group(1)` for one group and `.groups()` for all of them.
sections.code:
const text = "Order ORD-48213 shipped, ORD-50077 pending"

/ORD-\d{5}/.test(text)              // true
text.match(/ORD-\d{5}/)[0]          // "ORD-48213" (first match only)
text.match(/ORD-\d{5}/g)            // ["ORD-48213", "ORD-50077"]
for (const m of text.matchAll(/ORD-(\d{5})/g)) console.log(m[1])   // 48213, then 50077
text.replace(/ORD-(\d{5})/g, "#$1") // "Order #48213 shipped, #50077 pending"

const re = /ORD/g
re.test(text)   // true   (lastIndex is now 9)
re.test(text)   // true   (found the second ORD, lastIndex 28)
re.test(text)   // false  (no more matches, lastIndex resets to 0)
sections.pitfall: Writing Python patterns without the r prefix. In a normal string "\b" is a backspace character, so re.search("\bcat\b", s) silently never matches, while r"\bcat\b" works.

activity.title: The re module
activity.prompt: Run the code and match each output line to the call that produced it. Then remove re.MULTILINE from the findall call and predict the new first line before you run it again.

props.code:
import re

log = """2026-10-15 ERROR disk full
2026-10-15 info started
2026-10-16 Error timeout"""

print(re.findall(r"^\S+ error", log, re.IGNORECASE | re.MULTILINE))
print(re.match(r"\d+", "abc 123"))
print(re.search(r"\d+", "abc 123").group())
print(re.fullmatch(r"\d{4}", "12345"))
print(re.sub(r"(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})", r"\3/\2/\1", "2026-10-15"))
props.task: Remove re.MULTILINE, predict the first line, then run it.

check.question: In Python, which function checks that an entire string matches a pattern?
check.explanation: re.fullmatch succeeds only if the pattern covers the whole string. re.match anchors only the start, so re.match(r"\d{4}", "12345") still matches, and re.search looks anywhere.

sections.title: When not to use regex
sections.body:
Regex is a sharp tool, and an old joke applies: you had a problem, you used a regular expression, and now you have two problems. Knowing when to stop is part of the skill.

Reach for something else when:

- **The format is nested or structured.** HTML, XML and JSON nest to any depth, and regular expressions cannot count matching open and close tags. Use a real parser: `json.loads` or `JSON.parse`, an HTML parser such as BeautifulSoup or the browser's DOM, and the `csv` module for CSV with quoted fields.
- **A plain string method says it better.** `name.endswith(".csv")`, `"@" in email`, `line.startswith("#")` and `text.split(",")` are clearer and cannot hide escaping bugs.
- **The full rule is enormous.** A regex that truly follows the email standard runs to hundreds of characters. In practice, check something simple like `^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$` and then send a confirmation email, the only real proof that an address works. Dates are similar: `\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}` accepts `2026-13-45`, so validate with a date library.
- **Speed and safety matter.** Patterns with nested quantifiers such as `(a+)+$` or `(.*)*` can take exponential time on input that *almost* matches, because the engine tries every way of splitting the text before giving up. On a server, attacker-supplied input can freeze a process this way, an attack called **ReDoS** (regular expression denial of service). Avoid nested quantifiers over the same characters, prefer negated classes and limit input length.

When regex *is* the right tool, keep it maintainable. Test it against lists of strings that should and should not match (exactly what the tester puzzles do), keep patterns short or split them up, and comment them. Python's `re.VERBOSE` flag lets a pattern span several lines with whitespace and `#` comments, as in the example.
sections.code:
import re, json

# Hard to read
phone = re.compile(r"^\(?(\d{3})\)?[ -]?(\d{3})-(\d{4})$")

# The same pattern, documented with re.VERBOSE
phone = re.compile(r"""
    ^\(?(\d{3})\)?    # area code, optional parentheses
    [ -]?             # optional space or dash
    (\d{3})           # exchange
    -(\d{4})$         # line number
""", re.VERBOSE)
print(phone.match("(415) 555-0132").groups())   # ('415', '555', '0132')

# Structured data deserves a parser
data = json.loads('{"user": {"name": "Ada"}}')
print(data["user"]["name"])                      # Ada
sections.pitfall: Parsing HTML or JSON with a regex because the first test case worked. Real documents have nesting, attributes in any order and escaped quotes; a parser handles all of them.

check.question: What is the most reliable way to read user.name from a JSON API response?
choices: Parse it with JSON.parse or json.loads, then read the field
Capture it with a regex such as "name": "(.*)"
Split the response on commas and search each piece
Find the word name and take the next 20 characters
check.explanation: A parser understands nesting, escaped quotes and any key order. The regex breaks as soon as another "name" key appears, a value contains a quote, or the greedy .* runs past the closing quote.

keyTerms.definition: A pattern that describes a set of strings, used to search, validate and transform text.
A character with special meaning in a pattern, such as . * + ? ^ $ ( ) [ ] { } | and \.
A set in square brackets, like [a-z] or [^0-9], that matches exactly one character.
A repeat count for the item before it: *, +, ?, {n}, {n,m}.
Greedy quantifiers match as much as possible; adding ? makes them match as little as possible.
A zero-width position match: ^ for the start and $ for the end of the string (or line with the m flag).
\b, the position between a word character and a non-word character or the string edge.
Parentheses that group part of a pattern and save the matched text by number or name.
\1 inside a pattern: the same text that group 1 matched, repeated.
A zero-width check of what follows: (?=...) must match, (?!...) must not.
Regular expression denial of service: input that makes a badly written pattern backtrack for an exponential time.

summary: Literals match themselves; escape metacharacters such as . $ ( and + with a backslash.
A character class matches exactly one character; quantifiers repeat the single item before them.
Quantifiers are greedy; add ? for lazy, or use a negated class like [^>]+ to stop at a delimiter.
Anchor both ends with ^ and $ when validating, and use \b to find whole words.
Groups capture text for reuse, | has the lowest precedence, and lookarounds test without consuming.
Use raw strings in Python, watch the g flag's lastIndex in JavaScript, and use a parser for HTML, JSON and CSV.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend how a regex engine finds the match for `<.+>` in the text `bold`, step by step: why the result surprises people, and two different ways to make it match only ``.

questions.question: Which string does the pattern a.c NOT match?
questions.explanation: The dot must match exactly one character, and it can be any character except a newline: a letter, a real dot or a space. In "ac" there is nothing between a and c, so there is no match.

questions.question: Write a pattern that matches the text 3.14 but not 3x14 or 3-14.
questions.explanation: Escaping the dot with a backslash makes it match only a literal dot. Unescaped, 3.14 also matches 3x14 because . matches any character. 3[.]14 works too, since a dot inside brackets is literal.

questions.question: This should find prices like $25, but it never matches anything. Why?
choices: $ is the end-of-string anchor; escape it as \$ to match a dollar sign
The regex needs the g flag to search past the start of the string
test only checks the beginning of the string
questions.explanation: Unescaped, $ means the end of the input, and no digits can come after the end, so the pattern can never match. /\$\d+/ treats $ as an ordinary character. The g flag is not needed: without it the regex still searches the whole string and stops at the first match.

questions.question: What does [^0-9] match?
choices: Any single character that is not a digit
A digit at the start of the string
questions.explanation: A caret right after the opening bracket negates the class, so it matches one character that is not 0 through 9. It is still a single character, not a run, and ^ means start of string only outside brackets.

questions.question: What does this log?
questions.explanation: \d matches a single digit, and the g flag returns every match, so each of the six digits is its own match. With \d+ the runs would be grouped into 3 matches: "1", "22" and "333".

questions.question: Complete the pattern so it accepts strings made only of hexadecimal digits in either case, such as c0ffee or FF00AA.
questions.explanation: Several ranges can sit side by side in one class: 0-9, a-f and A-F. 0-F is a single range by character code, which also includes : ; < = > ? @ and misses lowercase letters. A comma inside brackets is literal, so 0-9,a-f would accept "1,2" and reject uppercase.

questions.question: What do \d, \w and \s match, and what do their uppercase versions match?
questions.answer: \d matches a digit, \w a word character (letter, digit or underscore), and \s a whitespace character. \D, \W and \S each match any single character that is not in the matching lowercase set.
questions.explanation: These shorthands are character classes, so each matches exactly one character. \d is the same as [0-9], and \D is the same as [^0-9].

questions.question: What does this expression return?
questions.explanation: .* is greedy: it runs to the end of the string, then backs up only until a closing " can match, which is the last quote in the string. So the match runs from the first quote to the last one, not just around "hi".

questions.question: What is the full match? Include the quote characters.
questions.explanation: *? is lazy: it takes as few characters as possible, so the match ends at the first closing quote. The negated class "[^"]*" gives the same result without relying on laziness.

questions.question: Which pattern matches both "color" and "colour" but not "colouur"?
questions.explanation: ? makes the u optional: zero or one. * allows any number, so it also matches colouur; + needs at least one u, so it misses color; and col.r allows exactly one character between l and r, so it misses colour.

questions.question: A PIN must be exactly 4 digits, but this check accepts "12345" and "PIN1234". What is the fix?
choices: Write \d{4,4} so the count is exact
Add the g flag so the whole string is checked
Anchor it as /^\d{4}$/ so nothing can come before or after
questions.explanation: Without anchors, test succeeds if four digits appear anywhere in the input. ^ and $ force the whole string to be exactly those four digits. {4,4} means the same as {4}, the g flag only affects finding multiple matches, and \d never matches letters.

questions.question: What does this expression return?
questions.explanation: \b only requires a boundary before the a. "art" and the start of "artist" both qualify, but in "party" the a follows p, a word character, so there is no boundary there. A second \b after art would leave only the whole word.

questions.question: Complete the pattern so only the standalone word "is" is replaced, giving "this was it".
questions.explanation: \b on both sides requires is to be a whole word, so the is inside "this" is skipped. Plain is replaces both ("thwas was it"), ^is$ needs the entire string to be is, and \sis\s also replaces the spaces ("thiswasit").

questions.question: Which string does ^cat|dog$ match that ^(cat|dog)$ does not?
questions.explanation: | has the lowest precedence, so ^cat|dog$ means "starts with cat" or "ends with dog", and catapult starts with cat. The grouped version requires the whole string to be exactly cat or dog. dogma matches neither: it does not start with cat or end with dog.

questions.question: What string does this return?
questions.explanation: The three groups capture 2024, 06 and 15 in order. The replacement inserts them as $3/$2/$1, which reverses the order and swaps the dashes for slashes.

questions.question: Complete the pattern so it matches a word in matching quotes, like 'hi' or "hi", but rejects mixed quotes like 'hi".
questions.explanation: \1 is a backreference: it must match the same text group 1 captured, so the closing quote has to repeat the opening one. ['"] or a new group accepts either quote, so 'hi" would pass, and $1 is replacement-string syntax that means end of string followed by 1 inside a pattern.

questions.question: What does this log?
questions.explanation: (?:...) groups without capturing, so the (\d+) after the dot is group 1, and it matched 15. If the first group captured, m[1] would be "2".

questions.question: Outside a character class, which of these characters must be escaped with a backslash to match themselves? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The dot, star and question mark are metacharacters, so they need \., \* and \?. Letters, the underscore and a hyphen outside brackets are ordinary literals.

questions.question: Match each pattern piece to what it matches.

pairs.right: One character that is not a lowercase vowel
One or more lowercase letters in a row
Any one character except a newline

questions.explanation: Brackets make a one-character set and a leading ^ negates it. The + after [a-z] is what turns one letter into a run of letters.

questions.question: What is the first match of `\d{3,5}` in the text `1234567`?
questions.explanation: The match starts at the leftmost possible position, and the greedy {3,5} takes as many digits as it is allowed: five. The lazy form \d{3,5}? would stop at 123.

questions.question: Why can `^(a+)+$` freeze a program when tested against 30 a's followed by an exclamation mark?
choices: The ! is a metacharacter that sends the engine into an endless loop
The $ anchor makes the engine reread the input once for every a
Nested quantifiers allow exponentially many ways to split the a's, and all are tried
Greedy quantifiers always take quadratic time on repeated letters
questions.explanation: The match must fail at the !, but before giving up the engine backtracks through every way of dividing the a's between the inner and outer +, roughly 2^30 attempts. Each extra a doubles the time. ^a+$ means the same thing and fails instantly.

questions.question: Which pattern accepts a string only if it is exactly a 3-letter uppercase code, like SFO?
questions.explanation: Validation needs both anchors and an exact count. [A-Z]{3} also accepts SFOX or xSFO, ^[A-Z]+$ accepts any length, and \b[A-Z]{3} accepts SFOX.

questions.question: What does this log?
questions.explanation: The named group month captured the two digits after the first dash. Named groups are read from match.groups in JavaScript; Python writes them (?P<month>...) and reads match["month"].

questions.question: What does this expression return?
questions.explanation: The lookahead only checks that EUR follows; it is not part of the match. 100 is followed by USD, so the first place where digits are followed by EUR is 200.

questions.question: Complete the pattern so it requires at least 8 characters, at least one uppercase letter and at least one digit.
questions.explanation: A second lookahead runs from the same starting position and adds the digit rule. (?!.*\d) would forbid digits, (?<=\d) looks behind the start where there is nothing, and \d+ would consume digits, forcing the string to begin with them.

questions.question: Which string does `^(?!test)\w+$` fail to match?
questions.explanation: The negative lookahead sits at the start, so it rejects only strings that begin with test. contest and attest contain test later, and Test differs in case (there is no i flag), so all three match.

questions.question: Match each flag to what it does.

pairs.right: Find every match, not just the first (JavaScript)
Let ^ and $ match at the start and end of each line
Let the dot match newline characters too

questions.explanation: These four cover almost every real need. In Python they are spelled re.IGNORECASE, re.MULTILINE and re.DOTALL; "find every match" is re.findall or re.finditer rather than a flag.

questions.question: What does this Python code print?
questions.explanation: re.match only tries at the start of the string, where "abc" is not a digit, so it returns None. re.search scans the whole string and finds 123.

questions.question: Complete the call so it returns `['1', '22', '333']`.
questions.explanation: \d+ matches each run of digits. \d returns single digits (six items), \w+ includes the letters (a1, b22, c333), and \d* also returns an empty string at every position without a digit.

questions.question: What does this log?
questions.explanation: With the g flag, test saves the position after a match in lastIndex. The second call starts searching after the a in "cat", finds nothing, returns false and resets lastIndex to 0. Use a regex without g for repeated test calls.

questions.question: What string does this return?
questions.explanation: Group 1 captures ada and group 2 captures example. The replacement r"\2:\1" writes group 2, a colon, then group 1.

questions.question: For which of these tasks is a regex alone a poor choice? Select all that apply.
choices: Extracting links from a full HTML page
Reading a field from a JSON API response
Checking that a string is exactly five digits
Validating email addresses against the full standard
Finding the lines that contain ERROR in a log
Splitting CSV lines whose quoted fields contain commas
questions.explanation: Nested or quoted formats need parsers (an HTML parser, json, csv), and the complete email grammar is impractical as a regex. Five digits (^\d{5}$) and log lines with ERROR are exactly what regex does well.

questions.question: In Python, what is the simplest correct way to check that `filename` ends with .csv?
questions.explanation: endswith says exactly what you mean. The search version has an unescaped dot and no anchor, so it matches "mycsvdata.txt"; re.match anchors at the start, so it only matches a file named exactly csv; and find matches csv anywhere.
